s: A shape with three straight *sides* is a *triangle*. Where two sides meet, there is a *corner*. A triangle has three corners. A square has four equal sides and four square corners. A rectangle has four sides too, but two are long and two are short.
m: Some shapes have more sides. A shape with five straight sides is called a pentagon. Home plate in baseball has five sides. Count them in a photo of a baseball field. A flat shape with straight sides has as many corners as sides.

s: A shape with six straight sides is a *hexagon*. It has six corners too. A clock face is round, with no straight sides and no corners. That shape is a *circle*. Size does not change a name. A tiny triangle and a huge triangle are both triangles.
m: Hexagons are useful. Many nuts that screw onto bolts have six sides, and a wrench grips those sides. Now look for circles. A wheel, a coin and a plate are all circles. How many circles can you find in your kitchen?

s: A dice is a *solid* shape. You can hold it, so it takes up space. It is a *cube*. A cube has 6 faces, and every face is a square. A ball is a solid shape too. It is round all over, with no flat faces. That shape is a *sphere*.
m: Look closer at a cube. Where two faces meet, there is an edge. A cube has 12 edges and 8 corners. Run a finger along the edges of a box shaped like a cube. A marble and a soap bubble are shaped like spheres too.

s: A can of soup is a *cylinder*. It has a circle on top, a circle on the bottom and a curved side. A party hat is a *cone*. It has one flat circle and a point on top. Two circles means a cylinder. One circle and a point means a cone.
m: You can find these shapes at home. A pipe, a can of corn and a straight drinking glass are cylinders. A traffic cone is a cone. It stands well because it rests on its wide circle, not on its point.

s: Shapes can *join* to make new shapes. Two same-size squares side by side make a rectangle. Cut a square from corner to corner and you get two triangles. Put them together and the square is back. Six triangles with their points in the middle make a hexagon.
m: Builders and children join shapes all the time. A simple drawing of a house is a square with a triangle on top. Together they make a new shape with five sides.
A tangram is an old puzzle. Its seven flat pieces fit together to make a square or many other pictures.

s: A *rule* tells you what a shape must have. The rule "four sides" fits a square and a rectangle. The rule "three sides" fits a triangle, tall or short. A shape with a curved side is not a square. Sides must be straight.
m: A rule can be about corners as well as sides. The rule "no corners" fits a circle. The rule "six sides" fits a hexagon. Some rules fit many shapes. Try it with a friend. One of you says a rule. The other draws a shape that fits. Then trade.

s: Shapes are on every street. A window is a rectangle and a manhole cover is a circle. Floor *tiles* are often squares. They fit with no gaps because their corners are square. A trash can is a cylinder. A ball in the park is a sphere.
m: Builders also choose shapes for strength. Many bridges and roofs have triangles in them. A triangle holds its shape when you push on it. A rectangle made of sticks with loose corners can tilt sideways. Next time you cross a bridge, look for triangles.

s: Fold a paper circle so the edges match. The fold makes two *equal* parts, the same size. Each part is one *half*. Two unequal pieces are not halves. Halves must be equal. Put the halves back together and the whole circle returns.
m: We use halves every day. Half past three means thirty minutes after three, because thirty minutes is half of an hour. You can take half of a group too. Half of 10 crayons is 5 crayons. Both halves must have the same number.

s: Cut a square straight down the middle. You get two tall rectangles. Each is a half. Cut a same-size square from corner to corner. You get two triangles. Each is a half too. They look different, but they are the same size. Halves of the same whole are always equal in size.
m: A circle can be cut in half in many ways. Any straight cut through the middle of a circle makes two halves. Turn the cut a little and it still works. A pizza cut through the center in any direction gives two equal halves.

s: Three friends share a granola bar. They cut it into three equal pieces. Each piece is one *third*. To make thirds, make two cuts, not three. Two cuts make three pieces. Three thirds make one whole.
m: We write one third as 1/3. Cooks use a one-third measuring cup in recipes. A third of an hour is 20 minutes. A round pizza can be cut into thirds too. Three slices of the same size meet in the middle.

s: Four kids share a small pizza. They cut it into four equal slices. Each slice is one *fourth*. Another name for one fourth is one *quarter*. Four fourths make one whole. More parts means smaller parts, so one fourth is smaller than one half.
m: We write one fourth as 1/4. A quarter coin is worth 25 cents. A quarter of an hour is 15 minutes. Cooks use a one-quarter measuring cup in recipes too.

s: A chocolate bar is made of small squares. They go across in *rows* and up and down in *columns*. A bar with 2 rows of 3 squares has 3 + 3 = 6 squares. A bar with 3 rows of 4 squares has 4 + 4 + 4 = 12. Adding by rows is faster than counting one by one.
m: Rows and columns are everywhere. Many egg cartons hold a dozen eggs in 2 rows of 6. A window may have panes in rows and columns. Seats in a theater are in rows too. Counting by rows helps you count big groups fast.

s: Count the people. Then cut that many equal parts. That is a *fair share*. Two kids share a pancake in halves. Three kids share it in thirds. Four kids share it in fourths. Two big pieces and one small piece are not thirds, so it is not fair.
m: There is a trick for fair cutting. One person cuts. The other person chooses first. The one who cuts will try hard to make the pieces equal, because they might get the smaller one. Try it with a friend and a cookie.
